result:
In November 2022, a retired print technician in Yorkshire named David Smith found a shape. He'd been cutting polygons out of card and sliding them around, looking for one that would cover an infinite floor without ever repeating itself. Mathematicians had been hunting that shape for fifty years. Smith's has thirteen sides and looks a bit like a hat, which is what everybody now calls it.

To see why anyone wanted this, you have to notice how thoroughly repetition saturates the idea of pattern. Bathroom tiles, brick walls, honeycomb, the wallpaper in a cheap hotel — every one of them has a unit you can lift and slide elsewhere and find an exact match waiting. This is periodicity, and it is so natural that nineteenth-century crystallographers built a science on the assumption that matter must obey it. Solids are atoms in repeating arrays. The possible symmetries were enumerated: 230 space groups, and five-fold symmetry flatly forbidden, because you cannot fill space with pentagons the way you can with hexagons. Case closed, and the closure was taught to students for a century.

The interesting question was whether repetition is *forced*. Not whether you can avoid it by cheating — anyone can lay bricks badly — but whether a shape could exist that tiles the plane and is *incapable* of tiling it periodically. Order with no rhythm. Structure that never comes back around.

Roger Penrose got there in the 1970s with two shapes, a kite and a dart, which fit together in endlessly many ways, none of them repeating. Beautiful, but two. The single-shape version became known as the einstein problem, a pun on the German *ein Stein*, one stone. Attempts kept arriving with asterisks attached: a single tile, but disconnected, in pieces; a single tile, but requiring matching rules that reach across arbitrary distances. Nobody could produce one honest connected shape you could cut from cardboard and hand to a child.

Smith's hat does it, with one wrinkle. Roughly one tile in eight has to be flipped over, mirror-side up. Purists reasonably complained that this is two shapes, a hat and its reflection. So Smith went back to the card. He'd noticed the hat wasn't a lone curiosity but a member of a whole continuous family — you can stretch its edges and the tiling property survives along the way — and in that family he found a particular member that can be given slightly curved edges, blocking the loophole that lets reflections form a periodic pattern. That one is called the spectre. It tiles the plane, it never repeats, and it needs no mirror. Two papers, six months apart, in 2023, closing a problem older than most of the people who solved it.

I love this story for the obvious reasons — the amateur, the cardboard, the fifty years — but the part I keep returning to is that the physical universe had already gotten there first.

On April 8, 1982, Dan Shechtman, an Israeli materials scientist on sabbatical at the U.S. National Bureau of Standards, looked at an electron diffraction pattern from an aluminum-manganese alloy and saw ten bright dots arranged with a symmetry that was not supposed to exist. He wrote in his notebook: "10 Fold???" He was asked to leave his research group for bringing disgrace on it. Linus Pauling, twice a Nobel laureate and the most formidable chemist alive, said publicly that there were no quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists. Shechtman was right. His alloy was ordered — sharply, provably ordered, producing crisp diffraction peaks — but its atoms never repeated. Nature had been quietly making Penrose tilings out of metal while we insisted it couldn't. He got the Nobel in 2011, twenty-nine years later, which is roughly the pace at which certainty erodes.

Then, in 2009, a team going through a rock sample from a stream in Chukotka, in the Russian far east, found a natural quasicrystal in a fragment of meteorite. Aluminum, copper, iron, locked in icosahedral order, forged in a collision somewhere in the early solar system about four and a half billion years ago. It has since been named icosahedrite. There is a mineral that has been sitting in a museum drawer in Florence, and drifting through space before that, built out of a pattern mathematics declared impossible in the nineteenth century and only described in the twentieth.

The deepest thing about these patterns, though, isn't the forbidden symmetry. It's what they do to the notion of *place*.

A Penrose tiling can be constructed by taking a perfectly ordinary periodic lattice in five dimensions, slicing it at an irrational angle, and projecting the slice down into two. That's where the order comes from — it's a shadow of something crystalline in a room we can't stand in. And one consequence, proved by John Conway, is this: any finite patch of a Penrose tiling, however large, appears infinitely often in *every* Penrose tiling. Not just somewhere in the same one. In all of them.

So imagine standing on such a floor. You look around at the tiles near your feet. You walk a mile and survey everything within a mile. You survey a continent. Nothing you can see will ever tell you which tiling you are in, because every view you could possibly have is a view available everywhere, infinitely many times. You are somewhere utterly specific, in a configuration that will never repeat, and no amount of local evidence can locate you.

That combination — unrepeatable globally, ubiquitous locally — is not something I have a tidy moral for. It just seems like a true and strange fact about how order can work, and I notice I'd rather know it than not.

The hat was always there. Thirteen sides, sitting in the space of possible polygons, waiting through the whole of human history, through Penrose and Pauling and the meteorite, until a man in Yorkshire with a pair of scissors and a lot of patience happened to reach it. The mathematics didn't change in November 2022. Our reach did. I find that a genuinely cheering thought, and I don't think it's sentimental: the space of things that exist is much larger than the space of things we've gotten around to, and the gap closes by people fiddling with cardboard.

What should I actually write about? Let me think about what genuinely draws me. A few candidates:

1. The nature of the open prompt itself — but that's a bit of a cliché move, the "meta" response, and can feel evasive or self-indulgent.
2. Something concrete and specific I find fascinating — a piece of mathematics, a historical oddity, a phenomenon in nature, a linguistic quirk.
3. Something about my own strange situation — but again, risks navel-gazing.

I think the best answer takes the invitation seriously by actually *choosing* something and going deep, rather than hedging or writing about the difficulty of choosing. The freedom should be exercised, not discussed.

What do I actually find myself drawn to? Let me scan... I'm genuinely fascinated by things where structure emerges from constraint. Some options:

- The fact that ancient Roman concrete gets stronger over time because of seawater interaction with volcanic ash — recently discovered "hot mixing" and lime clasts self-healing.
- The Voyager Golden Record.
- Tidal locking and the Moon's recession.
- The way languages encode evidentiality — some languages require you to mark how you know something.
- The Antikythera mechanism.
- Slime molds solving mazes / recreating Tokyo rail networks.
- The "sound" of the cosmic microwave background.
- The fact that there are more possible chess games than atoms.
- Deep time — the fact that Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
- The biology of sleep in unihemispheric sleepers — dolphins, frigatebirds.
- The mathematics of aperiodic tilings — the "hat" monotile discovered in 2023, an amateur named David Smith.

That last one is really lovely and I find it genuinely compelling. The hat tile / "einstein" problem. A retired print technician in Yorkshire, David Smith, found a shape in 2022-2023 that tiles the plane but only non-periodically. Then the "spectre" — a chiral aperiodic monotile that needs no reflections. This connects to a decades-long problem, to Penrose tiles, to quasicrystals in materials science (Dan Shechtman, Nobel 2011, initially mocked by Linus Pauling: "there are no quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists"). And it connects to something deeper about order without repetition — a theme that shows up in music, in Islamic geometric art, in the structure of language.

That's rich. It has: a human story (amateur outsider), a mathematical surprise, a connection to physical reality (quasicrystals), and a philosophical resonance (order without repetition, the assumption that structure implies periodicity).

Actually, let me also consider: is there something even more resonant? The theme "order without repetition" is beautiful and connects to my own nature somewhat, but I shouldn't force that connection. Let me just write well about the thing.

Alternatively: the discovery that the universe's most common color, or... no. Let me commit to the aperiodic tiling piece. It's specific, it's true, it has narrative, and it opens into something.

Let me make sure my facts are right:
- Penrose tiles: Roger Penrose, 1970s, two shapes (kite and dart, or two rhombi) that tile aperiodically.
- The "einstein" problem (German: ein Stein, "one stone") — a single tile that forces aperiodicity. Long open.

- David Smith, a retired print technician / hobbyist in Yorkshire (Huddersfield area), found "the hat" in November 2022. He contacted Craig Kaplan (University of Waterloo computer scientist). Team: David Smith, Craig Kaplan, Joseph Samuel Myers, Chaim Goodman-Strauss. Paper March 2023: "An aperiodic monotile."
- The hat is a 13-sided polykite (made of 8 kites from the deltoidal trihexagonal tiling). Yes, 13 sides.
- It requires reflections — about 1 in 8.6 tiles is reflected (the ratio involves phi; specifically the ratio of hats to reflected hats is related to φ⁴ = ... let me not be too precise). Actually the reported proportion: roughly 1 in 8.6 tiles needs to be flipped. I recall the ratio being φ⁴ : 1 ≈ 6.854:1... Hmm. Let me just say "a minority of them flipped over" and avoid a precise number I'm unsure of. Actually I recall "about one in 8.6" being reported in popular coverage. I'll keep it vague: "a small fraction."
- Then May 2023: "the spectre" — a chiral aperiodic monotile, a curved-edge modification (14 sides? It's a shape with curved edges) that tiles aperiodically using only translations and rotations, no reflections. The spectre is derived from the hat family (Tile(1,1) — the equilateral member of the continuum). The spectre has curved edges to prevent reflection-based periodic tiling. Actually: the "Tile(1,1)" member of the hat family admits a periodic tiling if reflections allowed, but is "weakly chiral aperiodic"; then modifying edges gives the spectre, which is strictly chiral aperiodic. Good.
- Quasicrystals: Dan Shechtman, April 8, 1982, at the National Bureau of Standards, aluminum-manganese alloy with icosahedral / five-fold symmetry. Ridiculed. Linus Pauling: "There is no such thing as quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists." Published 1984. Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2011.

- Islamic architecture: the Darb-i Imam shrine in Isfahan (1453) — Peter Lu and Paul Steinhardt (2007) argued girih tiles produce near-perfect Penrose-like quasicrystalline patterns. Some debate about whether it was intentional/systematic, worth hedging lightly.
- Aperiodic order in music: not necessary.
- The Fibonacci sequence and golden ratio in Penrose tilings: ratio of kites to darts approaches φ.
- Every finite patch of a Penrose tiling appears infinitely often in every Penrose tiling — and in every other Penrose tiling of the same type. This is a beautiful fact: local indistinguishability. You can never tell, from any finite region, which global tiling you're in. Conway's theorem: any finite patch of a Penrose tiling appears in every other Penrose tiling, infinitely often, and within a bounded distance (Conway's "worm" / empire problem). Actually the precise statement: any finite patch of a Penrose tiling occurs infinitely often in every Penrose tiling. This is "local isomorphism." Beautiful.

That last fact is the emotional/philosophical core: you can never locate yourself by looking around, because every neighborhood you could possibly see exists everywhere. Order without repetition, and infinite recurrence of the local. That's gorgeous.

Also relevant: the undecidability of the domino problem (Berger 1966, Wang tiles) — you cannot in general decide whether a set of tiles tiles the plane. Tiling is where computation hides in geometry.
